Max Common Chord 4

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Drag the dots to see a hidden circle that passes through five points.
How to play: Drag P, Q, A or B, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the statements, the hint or the names.
Look for the math

Two circles meet at P and Q. Extend the lines from P through the two centres, and five of the labelled points turn out to sit on one more circle. Here is why, and where the claim needs care.

Two circles, four more points

The centres are E and F. The line EP meets the first circle again at G and the second at M; the line FP meets the first circle again at L and the second at H. The applet constructs L and M as the other crossings of the circles C(E), C(F) and the circle through E, Q and F; this puts M on line EP and L on line FP, just as the page says. G and H are the antipodes of P: each is twice a radius away from P along the line to its centre.

Equal apex angles

Both isosceles triangles ELP and FMP have two equal sides, because E and F are centres. Their base angles at P are the two angles made by the crossing lines EP and FP, so those base angles are equal. Equal base angles force equal apex angles: ∠LEP = ∠MFP. In the starting picture both are about 51.4°. The status line recomputes them after every drag.

One circle through five points

Since L, E, P are collinear, ∠LEP is the same angle as ∠LEM; likewise ∠MFP = ∠LFM. So E, F, L and M form a cyclic quadrilateral. The page goes on to show that Q belongs to that same circle. This part holds for every non-degenerate position the logic test tried: the five points stayed on one circle to within a ten-thousandth of a unit.

Half the angle at Q

An inscribed angle is half the central angle over the same chord, so ∠LQP = ½∠LEP and ∠MQP = ½∠MFP when Q lies on the large arc. The page states those equalities without that condition, and also claims ∠LQP = ∠MQP and ∠LQM = ∠LEM. The sweep found that this is true in the arrangement the page draws but not after every drag: when Q moves onto the small arc LP, ∠LQP becomes 180° − ½∠LEP and is the supplement of ∠MQP. The concyclicity and the equal apex angles never failed; the unqualified angle equalities did. Unlike the sibling applets, which seek the longest chord, a bisector or the tangency condition, this one is about those equal angles and the common circle.

Try this: tick statement 1 and statement 2, then drag Q slowly past the line LP and watch the status line switch from half the apex angle to its supplement.
